newsitem.title: GERMANY: Wet weather hampers late harvest effort in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Wet weather hampers late harvest effort in Germany.

text.p: HAMBURG, Sept 5 - German farmers are trying to speed up the grain harvest, but changeable weather has hampered their effort and so work may continue until mid-September, farm sources said.
Recent rains had affected wheat and rye quality, and meant some grain had to be dried after being brought in.
Trade buying was active as merchants moved to replenish depleted stocks, but large-scale marketing had yet to begin.
"Consumers are awaiting competitive offers from across Europe, where crops have been secured earlier and are generally ample," one analyst said.
"Farmers are not giving in to projected harvest pressure, they seem ready to store the grain on-farm," he added.
They were hoping that export demand on a tight world market would allow for a generous EU grain export policy to develop over the next few months.
Farmers were also reluctant to part with low quality grain that could be used in on-farm feed.
And German premium wheat was expected to be in demand in areas that faced shortages of quality grain.
The targeted 41 million tonne national grain crop, versus 39.9 million in 1995, would comfortably exceed domestic demand.
Following is a region-by-region update-
NORTHERN GERMANY
Harvesting in the most northerly state of Schleswig-Holstein was 80-90 percent complete, according to the Kiel chamber of agriculture.
Late wheat and rye needed drying to avoid storage losses and had low falling numbers, which indicated weak baking quality.
Winter wheat yields were in a 7.0-9.0 tonnes per hectare range. Producer prices of wheat were at 240-270 marks a tonne and rye at 225 marks.
Oats and spring barley showed average yields and were valued at 235 and 220 marks ex-farm respectively.
Lower Saxony, reported sharply lower qualities in late wheat and rye.
Sprouting threatened bread qualities in wheat.
EASTERN GERMANY
Harvest efforts focused on wheat, where three quarters of the crop still needed to be cut, said grain analyst Peter Gerl at the Berlin office of farm price and marketing institute ZMP.
"Qualities are receding as late wheat and rye start to sprout, this is a problem for falling numbers," he said.
"Demand for quality wheat will emerge and this could mean premiums for top qualities may widen, if required," he said.
"Remaining rye fields are partly lodged and qualities are very poor, but 90-95 percent has been harvested."
Farmgate prices of bread wheat were 260-320 marks, reflecting the wide variety of grades and qualities.
Feed wheat prices were falling fast amid EU volume pressure. Prices stood at 225-255 marks, with bread rye at 200-245 and barley at 205-240.
A Mecklenburg country merchant estimated wheat in that region, which is set for export to Poland, showed average yields of 7.0 tonnes per ha, versus 6.8 in 1995.
Because of poor weather, only two thirds of the 1.7 million tonne wheat crop (1.6 million last year) was bread wheat versus more than 80 percent in 1995. But protein levels were high.
The total eastern German grain crop might be 12.8 million tonnes after 13.6 million last year. Yields might be down at 5.3 tonnes per ha (6.0).
WESTERN GERMANY
Wheat yields along the Rhine and in North-Rhine Westphalia state were 8.5 tonnes per ha (7.9-8.1 in 1995) and rye 6.6-7.6 tonnes (up 10 percent), the regional agriculture chamber said.
Most wheat and rye escaped the bad weather, so quality was high.
Average winter barley yields of 6.5-6.9 tonnes were 0.2 tonnes below last year but above the long-term average.
Some 80 percent of rye escaped the wet weather from late August, so bread rye supplies were unusually plentiful.
SOUTHERN GERMANY
Some 30-40 percent of Bavaria's grain was still in the fields, the Munich farm ministry said.

Hopes of a 6.6-6.7 million tonne crop (6.0-6.1 million in 1995) following a 1.7 percent area increase and a 9.3 percent yield rise to 5.9 tonnes per ha might not be fulfilled because of late crop losses due to poor weather.
